newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Stay fully weighted in Dutch equities - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Stay fully weighted in Dutch equities - analysts.

text.p: Equity strategists are telling investors to remain fully weighted in Dutch shares in 1997, even though they expect the market here to move broadly in line with the rest of Europe after several years of strong outperformance.
Amsterdam has regularly outshone the major European bourses in recent years, though analysts and strategists say markets geared more to cyclical recovery might well do better this year.
But investors should not reduce exposure to the Netherlands to chase short-term gains elsewhere, they said, as Amsterdam's strong and stable track record will reward them in the long run.

"It's always quite dangerous to be too negative on the Netherlands because it has a great sector mix and one of the best risk/return trade-offs in the whole of Europe," said David Bowers, European equity strategist at Merrill Lynch.

Bowers said that while he and his colleagues were not particularly bullish about the Netherlands, it was difficult to argue a bear case for the country, adding that he could not imagine Merrill Lynch underweighting the Dutch market.
"In the short term somewhere like Italy might outperform, but in terms of volatility of return, the Dutch market's volatility is extraordinarily low," he said.

Roger Monson, chief equity strategist at Daiwa Europe, said he did not expect the Dutch bourse to produce any pyrotechnics this year but he recommended investors keep the Netherlands fully weighted at nine percent of a European equity portfolio.

"The Dutch market is not going to give you exciting overall performance but it will match European trends and because of the quality of the leading companies...it should be viewed as a quality anchor in a European portfolio," he said.
Frans van Schaik, chief Dutch equities strategist at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett, had a similar view on the outlook for 1997.

"We expect the Dutch market to perform in line with Europe. We've outperformed (the) FT Europe (index) for six years in a row now and I think 1997 will be a year in which we'll be more in tandem with the European average," he said.
Van Schaik added cyclical stocks would probably rally in anticipation of an earnings recovery and other markets would benefit more from this than the Netherlands.
This was because Amsterdam had a profusion of growth stocks in sectors such as finance, media, services and high-tech while cyclicals made up less than one eighth of the market.
Van Schaik said that by late 1996 the Dutch market's prospective 1997 price-earnings ratio had risen to 17.1, bringing it more into line with other European markets.
But on the basis of yield-ratios, the Dutch market still looked relatively inexpensive, he said, with 10-year bond yields currently some 2.2 times the average 1996 dividend yield.
Monson also noted that P/E multiples had caught up with the rest of Europe, adding that he had long thought Dutch shares did not deserve to be trading at a discount to other markets.
He added the steady Dutch economy and the predictability of company earnings were also pluses for the Amsterdam market.
"The Dutch market has one of the most highly predictable and steady earnings records in terms of consensus estimates being accurate after the fact," he said.
